### R0-01 · Quick review

What does `LIMIT 5` do, and why use it on a big table?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

It returns at most 5 rows. It lets you peek at the data without printing every row.

### R0-02 · Predict the output

Dataset `longlist0`:

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM "longlist" WHERE "translator" = NULL;
```
What is printed?

A. `2`
B. `0`
C. `78`
D. `ERROR: no such column`

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**B**. `= NULL` is never true, so nothing is counted. `IS NULL` would find 2.
</details>

<sub>Source: [lecture0 L598-606](../sources/lecture0.txt) *“We could use IS NULL to figure out if a value is null.”*</sub>

### R0-03 · Concept check

Which quotes go around what in SQLite?

A. Double quotes for strings, single quotes for column names
B. Double quotes for identifiers (tables, columns), single quotes for strings
C. Either, interchangeably
D. No quotes ever

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**B**. The lecture's style convention is `"title"` for identifiers and `'hardcover'` for strings. Mixing them up can silently change meaning (debugging D0-03).
</details>

<sub>Source: [lecture0 L306-315](../sources/lecture0.txt) *“double quotes for column names and single quotes for string names”*</sub>

### R0-04 · Predict the output

Dataset `longlist0`:

```sql
SELECT "title" FROM "longlist" WHERE "title" = 'pyre';
```
What is printed?

A. `Pyre`
B. `(no rows)`
C. `ERROR: no such column: pyre`

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**B**. `=` compares text exactly, including case. `LIKE 'pyre'` would match *Pyre* because LIKE ignores (ASCII) case.
</details>

<sub>Source: [lecture0 L963-971](../sources/lecture0.txt) *“So in this case, the equal is going to be case-sensitive.”*</sub>

### R0-05 · Predict the output

Dataset `longlist0`:

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*), COUNT("translator") FROM "longlist";
```
What is printed?

A. `78 | 78`
B. `78 | 76`
C. `76 | 78`
D. `76 | 76`

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**B**. COUNT(column) skips NULLs, and two books have no translator.
</details>

<sub>Source: [lecture0 L1336-1343](../sources/lecture0.txt) *“So COUNT, when given a column, counts only those that”*</sub>

### R0-06 · Concept check

`ORDER BY "rating" LIMIT 10` returns…

A. the 10 best-rated books
B. the 10 worst-rated books
C. 10 random books
D. an error: DESC is required

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**B**. ORDER BY is ascending (smallest first) by default. The lecturer got 3.05 … 3.42 at first and fixed it with DESC.
</details>

<sub>Source: [lecture0 L1002-1017](../sources/lecture0.txt) *“So let me show you that ORDER BY does by default sort from least to greatest.”*</sub>

### R0-07 · Predict the output

Dataset `longlist0`:

```sql
SELECT MAX("title"), MIN("title") FROM "longlist";
```
What is printed?

A. `A New Name: Septology VI-VII | Wretchedness`
B. `Wretchedness | A New Name: Septology VI-VII`
C. `The Adventures of China Iron | Tyll`

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**B**. On text, MAX and MIN compare alphabetically, not by length. MAX is the alphabetically last title.
</details>

<sub>Source: [lecture0 L1305-1325](../sources/lecture0.txt) *“So MAX seems to give us the lowest alphabetically”*</sub>

### R0-08 · Concept check

Which pattern matches exactly four-character titles beginning with T?

A. 'T%'
B. 'T___'
C. 'T_%'
D. '%T___%'

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**B**. Each `_` is exactly one character, while `%` is any run of characters (including none).
</details>

<sub>Source: [lecture0 L805-814](../sources/lecture0.txt) *“This is the only title that has T and then three characters after it.”*</sub>

### R0-09 · Quick review

What does `BETWEEN 2019 AND 2022` include?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

Both ends, so it is the same as `>= 2019 AND <= 2022`.
</details>

<sub>Source: [lecture0 L878-883](../sources/lecture0.txt) *“This is inclusive.”*</sub>
